summary: A CMOS-compatible normal-metal tunnel junction technology based on TiW/Al-AlOx/TiW trilayers has been demonstrated with wafer-scale yield and validated using Coulomb blockade thermometers down to 20 mK. The TiW electrodes suppress Al superconductivity via proximity effects while preserving the high-quality AlOx barrier, enabling zero-field operation of non-superconducting junctions across a broad cryogenic temperature range.
motivation: Practical applications spanning quantum information, thermometry, and nanoelectronics require non-superconducting tunnel junctions either standalone or integrated with superconducting circuits, but previous suppression strategies (magnetic fields, Mn doping, Cu proximity) suffer from integration incompatibility and scalability limitations.
method: A TiW alloy—a standard CMOS-compatible diffusion barrier—was integrated as the normal-metal electrode in place of Al in a trilayer stack with in-situ oxidized Al tunnel barriers; devices were characterized via room-temperature resistance scaling ($R = \rho_t/(d_J - \text{LWR})^2$ with $\rho_t = 6900$ to 21000 Ω μm$^2$ across three wafers) and low-temperature transport measurements of CBT arrays ($61 \times 20$ junctions, $E_c/k_B = 41.3$ mK).
result: CBTs remained strictly normal-conducting from 20 mK to 1 K with junction temperature $T_\mathrm{CBT}$ agreeing with a calibrated ruthenium-oxide thermometer to within 1% over nearly two orders of magnitude; application of parallel magnetic fields up to 1 T produced negligible deviation ($\lesssim 3\%$), confirming complete absence of superconductivity and demonstrating robust thermometry without external magnetic field suppression.
